extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous social sketches (fans of Dickensian satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance-extraction for producing or assessing comic social sketches in the Dickens/Sketches-by-Boz mode: vivid character portraits, ritualised scenes, ironic contrasts, and escalation of detail to produce humour. Emphasises concrete detail, repetition, dialect, and juxtaposition of decorum and chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied crowd/character mix as source of amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The body of the House and the side galleries are full of Members; some, with their legs on the back of the opposite seat; some, with theirs stretched out to their utmost length on the floor; some going out, others coming in; all talking, laughing, lounging, coughing, oh-ing, questioning, or groaning; presenting a conglomeration of noise and confusion…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a dense, heterogeneous assemblage of people performing small, specific, and contradictory actions to create comic bustle and social texture. Small eccentricities distributed across many characters (postures, gestures, noises) create cumulative humour. Contrast formal setting with informal behaviour (decorum vs. lounging, coughing, groaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorable comic character-by-repetition and fixed costume
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicholas: ‘has held the same place, dressed exactly in the same manner, and said precisely the same things, ever since the oldest of its present visitors can remember… An excellent servant Nicholas is—an unrivalled compounder of salad-dressing… and, above all, an unequalled judge of cheese.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a comic character a stable, repeated set of traits (dress, phrases, expertise) and let their immutability become humorous. Detail a small, oddly specific pride (e.g., being an unequalled judge of cheese) and show how it dominates their identity. Repetition of costume and speech builds recognisability and comic expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic servant-dynamics: witty repartee + stolidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jane ‘is no bad hand at repartees… cuts jokes with Nicholas, too, but looks up to him with a great deal of respect—the immovable stolidity with which Nicholas receives the aforesaid jokes… is not the least amusing part of his character.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair a sprightly, teasing character with a stolid foil to generate recurring small jokes. Use brief physical actions (a playful dig with a fork) and sharp, quotable retorts to create comic interplay. The contrast between showy liveliness and imperturbable calm heightens amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and hyperbole for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘An Irish Member would go up there, and eat more dinner than three English Members put together. He took no wine; drank table-beer by the half-gallon… And what was the consequence? Why, the concern lost—actually lost, sir—by his patronage.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply deliberate excess (eating more than three men, half-gallon beer) to make behaviour ludicrous. Tie the hyperbole to a mock-serious consequence (financial loss, reputational alarm) to amplify satire. Exaggeration works best when anchored in a concrete, domestic image (dinner, porter, tumbler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering institutional ritual to expose absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a charity dinner: stewards ‘in march fourteen stewards, each with a long wand in his hand, like the evil genius in a pantomime’; the chairman wandering into a ‘maze of sentences’ and the annual announcement of Her Majesty’s donation of 25_l._ which elicits ritual applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out the formal steps of a public ritual (procession, music, toasts, subscription list) in procedural detail, then highlight the emptiness, repetition, or theatricality to satirise it. Reproducing official language or formulae verbatim (toasts, lists) makes the mechanical quality visible and funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic escalation and timing in scene progression
rubrics_metrics.description: The singers ‘after “pitching” their voices immediately begin _too-too_ing most dismally…’ leading to cries of ‘Sh—Sh—waiters!’ then confused applause and ‘Encore!’—a rising chain of misguided reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage small misunderstandings and let them cascade: a false response prompts a stronger, more absurd reaction. Employ short beats (singer—applause—shush—mistaken hiss—encore) to build momentum; comedic payoff comes from the accumulating mismatch between intent and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between grand phrasing and trivial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Chairman’s pompous address wanders until it hits ‘constitutional sovereign of these realms’ and then announces Her Majesty’s routine donation of 25_l._—the dignity of language contrasts with the petty, repeated fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapose elevated rhetoric and ceremonious tone with petty, mundane, or repetitive results (small donation amounts, rote announcements). The mismatch exposes pretension and becomes comic when the climax is disappointingly ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character portrait by concrete, incongruous physical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The awkward man: ‘the wig, of a dark hue but indescribable colour… if it be naturally brown, it has acquired a black tint by long service… great blinker-like spectacles assist the expression of that most intelligent face… a countenance so expressive of the most hopeless extreme of heavy dulness.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, odd, and slightly grotesque physical specifics (miscolored wig, blinker spectacles, odd gait) plus a simile or paradox to embody a trait ( ‘hopeless extreme of heavy dulness’ ). Combining sensory detail and a telling comparison yields instantly comic portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nostalgic irony: lamenting lost romance to comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: On May Day: an ostensibly sentimental opening about spring and childhood quickly turns to ironic lament—‘Where are they now! Pillars we have, but they are no longer rustic ones; and as to dancers, they are used to rooms… Think of the immorality, too!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with sincere-sounding nostalgia then undercut it with pragmatic or absurd modern realities. The clash between idealised memory and contemporary banality produces wry humour. Use escalating examples of decline (from rustic pillars to register-stove-driven changes) to underline the irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialect and reported speech as comic authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sluffen’s speech in dialect: ‘That now he’d cotcht the cheerman’s hi, he vished he might be jolly vell blessed… he ’ad been a chummy—he begged the cheerman’s parding for usin’ such a wulgar hexpression—more nor thirty year—he might say he’d been born in a chimbley…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render a speaker’s voice through phonetic spelling and colloquial turns to convey class, profession, and comic self-importance. Use reported speech blocks for punchy, character-revealing monologues. Be mindful that dialect both entertains and reveals social position; proximity to character avoids caricature but highlights comedic traits.
